Definition: Height of cut. The blade height a lawn is mowed at, in inches or millimeters. Lower HOC suits reel-cut warm-season grasses; too low scalps.
Plant growth regulator, often trinexapac-ethyl, that slows vertical growth and increases density, stretching the interval between mows.
A herbicide applied before weed seeds germinate, timed by soil temperature or GDD, to prevent crabgrass and other annuals.
A herbicide applied to weeds that have already germinated and are actively growing.
Cutting too low in one pass, exposing stems or soil and stressing the turf. Also the intentional early-spring dormant scalp on Bermuda.
Mowing with a reel mower at very low HOC for a tight, striped, golf-green look. The enthusiast aspiration.
The crisp edge where turf meets hardscape or bed, created by edging. A signature flex in lawn culture.
Late-season fertilization while grass is entering or in dormancy, to support spring green-up.
Growing degree days. A heat-accumulation metric from daily temperatures that predicts growth rate and times applications better than a fixed calendar.
The light/dark pattern from bending grass blades in alternating directions with a roller or mower. The screenshot-bait pattern.
Nitrogen-Phosphorus-Potassium. The three numbers on a fertilizer bag, percentage by weight of each macronutrient.
A lab analysis of soil pH and nutrient levels that drives an accurate fertilization plan. Basis of the proprietary soil-kit data moat.
The layer of dead and living organic matter between green blades and soil. Excess thatch blocks water and air.
A mechanical removal of excess thatch with a dethatcher or vertical mower.
Sowing seed into existing turf to thicken it, or seeding ryegrass over dormant Bermuda for winter color.
Pulling soil cores or spiking to relieve compaction and improve water, air, and nutrient movement to the roots.
A warm-season grass dominant in the Sun Belt. Loves heat, tolerates low HOC, stripes beautifully. The launch-market hero grass.
A warm-season grass, dense and slow-growing, tolerant of a range of conditions. Common in the Sun Belt alongside Bermuda.
A warm-season grass with wide blades, common in the Gulf South. Mowed higher; does not take reel-low.
A cool-season grass, often tall fescue, common in transition and northern zones. Higher HOC; the northern-churn seasonality case.
Kentucky bluegrass. A cool-season grass prized for color and self-repair via rhizomes. Northern enthusiast favorite.
